item.title: AI giants agree on shared robots.txt token for publisher opt‑out
item.description:
AI giants agree on shared robots.txt token for publisher opt‑out

OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, and Anthropic announced they will adopt a new standard that lets publishers opt out of AI‑powered scraping via a shared signal placed in a site’s robots.txt file.

🔍 Overview

  • The biggest names in AI are backing a new way to opt out of scraping.
  • Publishers can apply their AI training preferences across multiple crawlers instead of setting them individually.
  • The signal lives within the existing robots.txt file, which already tells crawlers what they may or may not scrape.

🧩 How it works

  • A policy token is added to robots.txt; any AI crawler that respects the standard will read the token and honor the publisher’s preferences.
  • The token was proposed by Kevin Kelley, a technical lead for standards at Anthropic, as part of the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) process.
  • When a crawler encounters the token, OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, and Anthropic say they will restrict their AI crawlers from accessing the site.

⚙️ Key details

  • Meta: Communications head Andy Stone said, “We believe creating a common signal that conveys such preferences to multiple providers at once is an important step,” and added, “And we look forward to working with other AI companies on the standards and their implementation across the industry.” Meta has signaled support but has not confirmed whether it will honor the token.
  • Microsoft: Will offer granular controls that let publishers opt out of AI training or AI grounding. Sites will still appear in Bing search results regardless of their choices.
  • Google: Previously implemented similar controls that let sites block AI search features or training without affecting search visibility.
  • Existing efforts to curb unauthorized scraping include the Really Simple Licensing (RSL) standard, which lets publishers charge crawlers, and Cloudflare’s default blocking of AI crawlers.

🚀 Availability

Company Current status Planned rollout
Anthropic Already adopted the signal –
Google Will support the signal Next year
Microsoft Will support the signal Next year
OpenAI Will implement the signal Coming months

💡 Why it matters

  • Publishers no longer need to negotiate separate AI training preferences with each AI provider.
  • A single, standards‑based token simplifies compliance and reduces the administrative burden of managing many individual requests.
  • The move comes as publishers grapple with a continuing influx of AI crawlers that feed content into large language models.
  • Providing a common opt‑out mechanism could help balance the interests of content creators with the data needs of AI developers.

#OpenAI #AITraining #RobotsTxt #Publishing #IETF

Source: The biggest names in AI are backing a new way to opt out of scraping

item.title: Meta Delays New Business Terms Again Amid Publisher Concerns Over AI Training
item.description:
Meta Delays New Business Terms Again Amid Publisher Concerns Over AI Training

Meta has announced it may delay the implementation of its new business terms past the November 20th deadline as the company faces backlash from publishers regarding AI training practices. The company has stated it does not plan to implement these policy changes without a full consultation with industry groups and leaders, a process that may delay enforcement indefinitely.

🔍 Overview

  • Original Effective Date: October 30th.
  • First Delay: Postponed to November 20th.
  • Current Status: Likely to be delayed beyond November 20th as consultations continue.
  • Active Terms: Meta’s existing business terms will remain in place until the updated version is implemented.

⚙️ Key details

The controversy surrounds updated business terms that initially appeared to grant Meta permission to train its AI models on news sites that utilize Facebook and Instagram. While Meta later removed specific language regarding “training” products on content scraped from these sites, legal experts from Nieman Lab have noted that the updated policy still does not explicitly rule out the possibility.

Meta communications head Andy Stone addressed the situation on X, stating, “We’ve heard publishers’ feedback on our proposed ads and business terms update. We’re committed to getting this right, and as we expect this consultation could extend beyond November 20, in which case we’d delay implementation of the updated terms.”

💡 Why it matters

The proposed changes have drawn significant opposition from industry organizations and government officials who are concerned about the exploitation of content for AI development.

Stakeholder Position or Action
Andy Stone (Meta) Committed to a full consultation with industry leaders before policy changes.
Legal Experts (Nieman Lab) Noted that policy revisions are currently insufficient to rule out AI training.
News/Media Alliance Provided pushback against the proposed business terms.
Sen. Marsha Blackburn (R-TN) Stated the terms indicate Meta is attempting to exploit American creators and businesses.
Sen. Adam Schiff (D-CA) Urged Meta to reverse the proposed policy changes.

#Meta #AITraining #DigitalPublishing #TechPolicy

Source: Meta says it’ll probably delay its controversial new business terms again

item.title: Adaptive Teacher Supervision (GAD-RL) Boosts Vision-Language OCR Performance
item.description:
Adaptive Teacher Supervision (GAD-RL) Boosts Vision-Language OCR Performance

🔍 Overview

  • Vision‑language models can rewrite anomalous text in images into linguistically plausible expressions, which harms the faithfulness of OCR transcription.
  • Sequence‑level task rewards and local teacher guidance complement each other, but a fixed teacher’s guidance loses effectiveness as the student model improves, both across training checkpoints and across response groups with different task rewards.

⚙️ How it works

  • GAD‑RL (Adaptive Guidance Regulation for Reinforcement Learning) adjusts teacher supervision during joint post‑training based on the student’s current task performance and local output distributions.
  • A frozen teacher conditions on reference transcriptions and on prefixes generated by the student.
  • The method disables distillation for response groups that contain an output with a task reward of at least 0.95 and continuously attenuates the distillation strength as the group‑mean reward rises.
  • It also weights the forward KL term by the student’s probability of the teacher’s top‑1 token, reducing the impact of local auxiliary updates when the student gives low support to that candidate.

📊 Results

  • On the Qwen3.5‑2B model, GAD‑RL attains 59.92% Micro Recall on CHAOS‑Bench, outperforming:
    • GRPO by 8.45 percentage points,
    • GRPO+OPD (fixed‑weight) by 4.43 percentage points.
  • The same model reaches an Overall score of 91.18 on OmniDocBench v1.6.

💡 Why it matters

  • By dynamically scaling teacher supervision, GAD‑RL maintains effective guidance throughout training, preventing the degradation observed with static teachers.
  • The approach yields measurable gains on both micro‑level recall for OCR‑specific benchmarks and macro‑level performance across diverse document tasks, demonstrating that adaptive supervision can improve both fidelity and generalization in vision‑language systems.

#VisionLanguage #OCR #AdaptiveLearning #AITraining

Source: Improving OCR Faithfulness via Gated and Attenuated On-Policy Distillation Source: Training LLM Judges from Language Feedback via Position-Selective Self-Distillation

item.title: Ukraine Releases Millions of Drone Flight Data Points for AI Training
item.description:
Ukraine Releases Millions of Drone Flight Data Points for AI Training

Battlefields in Ukraine are littered with the remnants of drones, which are now firmly established as a critical weapon of modern warfare. The Ukrainian Ministry of Defense announced in January that it would make millions of data points gathered during tens of thousands of drone flights available to both military contractors and commercial companies.

🔍 Overview

  • The data includes images, video, controller inputs and other sensor streams collected on every flight.
  • More than 100 companies and the UK government have already gained access to the dataset.
  • The release is presented as a quick way for a country at war to attract funding and partnerships.

📊 Scale & Access

  • The Ministry’s program covers millions of data points from tens of thousands of flights.
  • Enabled Intelligence, an American data‑processing firm, has made over half a million hours of Ukrainian drone footage available for AI model training.
  • Access is granted to both defense firms and commercial enterprises.

🛠️ How It Works

  • Unmanned systems collect thousands of data points per flight, ranging from raw imagery to operator inputs.
  • The most valuable training moments are “exceptions”: loss of visibility, signal jamming, or human improvisation.
  • AI companies traditionally spend years and large sums to capture enough of these rare events; war generates them at a frequency that controlled testing cannot match.
  • Commercially available AI systems now allow inexpensive drones to operate autonomously or in coordinated flocks as the environment changes.

💰 Economic Impact

  • Battlefield data offers large volumes of machine experience gathered under conditions no laboratory can produce, creating immense financial value for defense firms.
  • By opening the dataset, Ukraine creates a revenue stream and partnership opportunities while supporting the development of next‑generation models for both military and commercial use.

🌐 Broader Implications

  • Earlier, American drones over Syria and Yemen supplied data that informed the first generation of semiautonomous military hardware in the late 2010s.
  • Drones trained in the signal‑jammed airspace over Ukraine are now being deployed in agriculture to map fields lacking cell signal.
  • Other countries are likely to follow Ukraine’s example, raising questions about a new data marketplace.
  • Purchase controls and intelligence vetting aim to mitigate the risk of bad actors acquiring the data, though the provenance of AI training data can become opaque once embedded in models.

📚 Future Outlook

  • Military programs such as Project Maven kept sensor‑heavy drone data within classified channels for internal weapons development. Ukraine’s open‑access model marks a shift toward broader civilian and commercial use of battlefield data.
  • As more nations consider monetising combat‑generated datasets, the industry will need new safeguards to track data lineage and prevent misuse.

#Ukraine #DroneData #AITraining #DefenseTech

Source: Data from drones in Ukraine is fueling a new Wild West marketplace

item.title: 🚀 No GPU Left Behind: How Co-located vLLM is Revolutionizing LLM Training Efficiency
item.description:
🚀 No GPU Left Behind: How Co-located vLLM is Revolutionizing LLM Training Efficiency

𝗦𝘂𝗺𝗺𝗮𝗿𝘆: Discover how the new co-located vLLM integration in TRL eliminates idle GPU time during GRPO training by running both training and inference on the same GPUs—delivering up to 1.73× speedup without sacrificing model quality, even on 72B parameter models.

🔍 The Training Bottleneck Problem

Training large language models using online learning methods like GRPO (introduced in the DeepSeekMath paper) requires constant generation of model outputs during the training loop. This creates a critical efficiency challenge: traditional setups force GPUs to take turns between training and inference tasks.

Before TRL v0.18.0, vLLM was only supported in server mode, running as a separate process on dedicated GPUs—creating a wasteful “ping-pong” pattern:

  1. Training GPUs run the model update step
  2. Training GPUs sit idle while waiting for generation
  3. vLLM server GPUs generate completions
  4. vLLM GPUs sit idle while training resumes
  5. Repeat…

This inefficient workflow results in:

  • 💸 Wasted GPU resources on both sides
  • 🔌 Increased hardware requirements
  • ⏱️ Reduced overall throughput
  • 📈 Higher training costs

🌟 Enter Co-located vLLM: The Game-Changer

The core innovation introduced in TRL PR #3394 is elegant yet powerful: run both training and inference on the 𝘀𝗮𝗺𝗲 GPUs.

Instead of operating as a standalone server process, vLLM now runs alongside the training code within the same distributed process group. The key advantages of this colocation approach:

  • Unified GPU Utilization: Training and inference share resources, taking turns efficiently without idle time
  • Direct Communication: Eliminates HTTP overhead by running vLLM in-process
  • Seamless Scaling: Works natively with torchrun for multi-node deployment
  • Full Parallelism Support: Compatible with both Tensor and Data Parallelism
  • Simplified Deployment: No separate server management needed

To enable this in your training pipeline, it’s as simple as changing one parameter:

1
2
3
4
5

training_args = GRPOConfig(
 ...,
 use_vllm=True,
 vllm_mode="colocate", # This enables colocation!
)

📊 Real-World Performance Gains

The team ran extensive experiments comparing traditional server mode to the new co-located approach. The results were impressive across various model sizes and configurations:

🔹 For Smaller Models (1.5B parameters)

  • Up to 1.43× speedup with larger batch sizes
  • Better performance with less tensor parallelism

🔹 For Medium Models (7B parameters)

  • 1.35× speedup at larger batch sizes
  • Performance improves with more tensor parallelism, reaching 1.73× speedup

🔹 For Massive Models (Qwen2.5-Math-72B)

  • Co-located setup achieves ~1.26× faster throughput even with 𝙛𝙚𝙬𝙚𝙧 GPUs
  • Equal model quality on Math500 benchmark compared to traditional training

One crucial innovation that enables efficient training of massive models is the integration of vLLM’s sleep() API into the training loop. This function temporarily frees GPU memory, allowing:

  • Level 1 Sleep: Unloads model weights but keeps them accessible in CPU memory
  • Level 2 Sleep: Completely unloads both weights and KV cache

For GRPO, which updates the model after every step, Level 2 sleep provides maximum memory efficiency, avoiding contention between training and generation tasks.

📈 Technical Implementation Details

The implementation combines several advanced techniques to maximize performance:

  1. Process Group Awareness: Co-located vLLM respects the torch.distributed process group:

2
3
4
5
6

if self.vllm_tensor_parallel_size > 1:
 self.tp_group, _ = torch.distributed.new_subgroups_by_enumeration(
 [
 list(range(i * self.vllm_tensor_parallel_size,
 (i + 1) * self.vllm_tensor_parallel_size))
 for i in range(self.accelerator.num_processes //
 self.vllm_tensor_parallel_size)
 ]
 )

  1. Memory Management: For large models like Qwen2.5-72B, DeepSpeed ZeRO Stage 3 optimizations handle memory constraints:

    • Offloading optimizer states to CPU
    • Overlapping communication with computation
    • Using contiguous gradients to reduce memory fragmentation

  2. Accelerate Integration: The whole system leverages HuggingFace’s Accelerate library for streamlined distributed training.

🔮 The Future of Efficient LLM Training

Despite a few challenges like occasional segmentation faults during shutdown (reported in Issue #16993), the co-located vLLM approach represents a significant advancement in LLM training efficiency.

The most important lessons from this work:

  • 🔥 Co-located inference dramatically improves GPU utilization without requiring additional hardware
  • 🧠 Memory management via vLLM’s sleep() is crucial for large-scale training
  • ⚡ The approach maintains model quality while delivering substantial throughput gains

This innovation makes training large models faster, cheaper, and more accessible—especially important as models continue to grow in size and complexity.

💡 Try It Yourself

Want to experience the efficiency gains firsthand? Here’s a minimal example to get started with GRPO training using co-located vLLM:

from datasets import load_dataset
from trl import GRPOConfig, GRPOTrainer

dataset = load_dataset("trl-lib/tldr", split="train")

def reward_len(completions, **kwargs):
 return [-abs(20 - len(completion)) for completion in completions]

training_args = GRPOConfig(
 output_dir="Qwen2-0.5B-GRPO",
 use_vllm=True,
 vllm_mode="colocate", # Enable colocation
 vllm_gpu_memory_utilization=0.3,
 max_steps=2,
 num_generations=4,
 per_device_train_batch_size=4,
)

trainer = GRPOTrainer(
 model="Qwen/Qwen2-0.5B-Instruct",
 reward_funcs=reward_len,
 args=training_args,
 train_dataset=dataset,
)

trainer.train()

As LLMs become increasingly central to AI advancement, innovations that maximize hardware efficiency will be crucial. The question is no longer just “how powerful is your model?” but also “how efficiently can you train it?”
